subsubtopic: REQUESTS CONCERNING FORMER AMBASSADOR LUCIEN BOUCHARD-DELAY IN RECEIVING ANSWERS
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, I have travelled across the country studying parole and sentencing. We have heard from a clear majority of Canadians of their concern about violent criminals not serving enough of their sentences.
I am encouraged by the proposals of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) that the time all federal inmates must serve before becoming eligible for parole will be increased and the system of earned remission, under which inmates can receive up to one-third of their sentences off for good behaviour, will be replaced.
The time is right, the Solicitor General says, for us to demonstrate our primary concern for public safety and our collective commitment to improving the system with that in mind. I hope we will see legislation brought forward in this House to ensure that public safety is first and foremost a consideration when looking at parole and sentencing.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY-UPGRADING REQUIRED IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government appears to be considering more spending on highways. Under agreements with each of the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, Transport Canada spent as much as $80 million in 1985-86 to improve the Trans-Canada Highway in each of these provinces. In 1987-88 Transport Canada added agreements with the four western province and spent $75 million on the Trans-Canada and Yellowhead Highways in nine provinces. The National Capital Commission similarly spent $69 million in highway construction in the 1979-87 period, all of it under joint projects with the Province of Quebec.
The federal Government is now apparently discussing twinning of the Trans-Canada Highway across Newfoundland, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has suggested federal assistance to complete the highway from Lac St. Jean to the James Bay power projects.
The people of Northern Ontario experience very little of southern Ontario's prosperity. They want the Trans-Canada Highway significantly upgraded through northern Ontario to encourage economic development in our region. The time has come for the federal Government to stop discriminating against northern Ontario in making agreements with the provinces to support highway improvement.

June 15, 1988

subsubtopic: BANFF-CITIZENS' VOTE IN FAVOUR OF SELF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Abraham Lincoln, in a speech in 1854 said: "No man is good enough to govern another man without that other's consent".
For 105 years, ever since Banff National Park was created, the people of Banff have been governed by a "Mayor" who lived in Ottawa 2,000 miles away. However, this week things have changed. The people of Banff voted for self-government and now the Mayor and Council of Banff will govern with the consent of the people and will be accountable to the people.
Self-government for Banff has been one of my objectives ever since I was a elected as their Member of Parliament. I want to thank our past "Mayor", the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), for his positive attitude and help, and a splendid school board, a visionary park warden and staff, the Chamber of Commerce, the Crag and Canyon, the Government of Alberta, and a host of Banff citizens for their tireless and relentless work which culminated in the favourable vote.
Ring out the old! Ring in the new!

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF SEWERS-NEED FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise again to speak on sewers and submarines. According to the Science Council of Canada, less than 60 per cent of Canadians are served by sewage treatment plants. In Quebec the number falls below 20 per cent, and in Newfoundland to 12.7 per cent.
Often untreated sewage is discharged into our rivers and lakes or pollutes ground water. Every summer, public beaches are closed. For example, in August, 1987, beaches in Toronto were posted as unfit for swimming because of the risk to health posed by polluted waters.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities urges every year that the federal Government pay a share of the $15 billion needed to help municipalities build the necessary sewers. Ottawa refuses. This Government does not believe clean water and sewage treatment are national priorities. Instead, it prefers to build nuclear submarines. What a perverse set of priorities! By contrast, the Liberal Party is committed to pay the federal share in order to provide Canadians with clean drinking water.

subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the three subsidiary agreements on official languages the federal Government has just signed with Saskatchewan concerns education in French.
To ensure that Francophones in Saskatchewan will be able to administer their own schools, the federal Government will provide financing of up to $26 million over a period of ten years.
The same agreement provides that $10 million will be provided over the next five years for a series of measures aimed at developing French educational services and offering Francophones better access to education in French.
The agreement also provides $17 million over a period of five years for establishing a language training institute that will play a major role in promoting French as the other official language.
Mr. Speaker, the agreements that have now been signed are not a panacea, but we must admit this is a very encouraging start, since the agreements concern education, an area vital to the existence of a language community.
Mr. Speaker, this is one more example of how the Progressive Conservative Government honours its commitments to the language minorities of this country!

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to read that on Saturday, June 4, 1988, the delegates attending the Baptist Convention of Ontario and Quebec annual assembly voted overwhelmingly to oppose any plans by the federal Government to recognize sexual orientation in the Canadian Human Rights Act. Mr. Speaker, Members on all sides of this House know that I have been doing my best to get help for the men and women who used to work at Massey Combine Corporation. They lost their jobs, medical benefits, and some pension income when the company went into receivership in March.

parachute to keep himself from ever losing his salary and benefits if something goes wrong at Varity. Mr. Rice can use this termination agreement to get four times his annual salary, plus a bonus.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL GOVERNMENT'S SIGNING OF AGREEMENTS WITH SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the federal Government has signed four landmark language agreements with the Province of Saskatchewan. These 10-year agreements, totalling some $60 million, are a good example of the Government's commitment to work with the provinces in a productive, co-operative, and progressive way.
The agreements include a commitment to enhance our already well-received French immersion programs in Saskatchewan schools, an excellent opportunity for all young people of our province. The federal contribution will allow for the translation of Saskatchewan's statutes and regulations, and for wider use of French in the courts, as well as assisting implementation of the management of French schools by the fransaskois community.
These agreements allow all people of Saskatchewan access to the language of their choice. I commend the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) for his hard work in securing these agreements, and I thank the province for its co-operation and assistance.

Madam
Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to rise to debate the motion which you have now ruled on to indicate the intention of the New Democratic Party to debate a variety of pieces of legislation which would come before the House of Commons.
Perhaps this would be a useful time to indicate that on many occasions I have made the point that we in the New Democratic Party are quite prepared to debate expeditiously appropriate issues as they come before the House and to pass them expeditiously, to move in a most co-operative way.
I will use as examples two items. Yesterday discussions occurred between the House Leaders of the Government, the Official Opposition, and the New Democratic Party as to whether or not it would be appropriate for us to extend the sittings of the House last night to allow all of those Members who wanted to participate in the Meech Lake Accord debate an opportunity to do so. That required a departure from the usual sitting hours. It required co-operation between the Government, the Liberals, and the New Democratic Party.
I felt that that was an appropriate initiative, that it was an important issue to deal with. There were Members from all Parties available to speak. That willingness resulted in a co-
June 15, 1988

operative decision between the three House Leaders representing the three political Parties to extend the debate into the evening and that was done.
A few days earlier willingness to co-operate was demonstrated when the Government House Leader inquired whether the opposition Parties would be prepared to consider as a package on the same day three different pieces of legislation dealing with native people in order to facilitate the passage of that legislation. As a matter of fact, I believe that one of the Bills was initiated by Chief Jules of the Kamloops Indian Band and was with regard to taxation on Indian lands.
That Bill moved through second reading, report stage, third reading, and Committee of the Whole all in one session. In addition, a number of other Bills were moved through various stages. That again demonstrated the willingness to co-operate on legislation which is obviously in the best interests of the country.
I could go on with a whole set of examples. As a matter of fact, I think the Government House Leader himself was indicating with some pride that in this session of Parliament we have passed more legislation than any session of Parliament in recent history. At the same time government Members say that the Opposition is holding up legislation. You cannot have it both ways, you cannot be passing extraordinary numbers of Bills and at the same time make a case that the Opposition is being obstructive. I want to make it clear that that is not the case.
There are Bills on the Order Paper which the Government has indicated interest in bringing forward and which we believe ought to have some debate and study in committee. They are Bills which we do not necessarily oppose in principle but would like to have improved. For that reason we are anxious to get on with it. However, the Government never brings them forward.
I use as an example the concerns of the disabled with regard to the National Transportation Act. We have been hearing for weeks that the disabled communities of the country want these changes to the National Transportation Act in order to facilitate movement of disabled people. We want to pass this legislation expeditiously and do what we can to co-operate. However, the Government never brings it forward and we cannot, therefore, co-operate. If the Government brought that legislation forward today, I can guarantee that we would pass it in 15 minutes. However, the Government does not bring it forward. It is fixated on the trade deal at the expense of all other legislation.
Today my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), said that if the Government brings forward a Bill such as the Private Member's Bill of the Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) to restrict the banks' ability to introduce service charges in the willy-nilly, comprehensive way in which they are, we will pass it in one hour. That is the kind of co-operation we are prepared to provide on this critical matter.

Madam Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to a specific Standing Order, 10(2), because that is really the one that has to be interpreted. It reads:
(2) Not more than two hours after the commencement of proceedings thereon, the Speaker shall put every question necessary to dispose of the said motion.
I think that we should take "after the commencement of proceedings" to mean two hours of actual debate. That is what it means. It means that the debate cannot take more than two hours. It does not mean that the debate cannot be interrupted by a lunch break or the normal adjournment of the House, like this evening, and be continued the next morning. What it means is that when Members have debated this question for a period of not more than two hours, the Chair has no choice.
The Speaker who is in the Chair must then rise, interrupt the proceedings and put every question necessary to dispose of the motion. I therefore maintain that since it is now after six o'clock-to continue along the same lines as my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier-the normal time for adjournment, the Chair should adjourn the House and continue tomorrow, in the first hour of the sitting, the debate on the motion very properly moved by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.
